verdict: OK to lend selectively in Panipat woollens — favour integrated, low-leverage units with fire compliance; avoid single-channel blanket makers exposed to the 50% domestic demand dip.
title: Panipat woollen & shawl textiles: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Panipat turns polyester yarn into mink, flano and polar blankets, and roughly 160 units here supply almost 99% of domestic demand [3].** Cash comes from four channels — stockists, the marriage season, festivals and cold weather [3] — so the year is a seasonal spike, not a smooth line. Yarn is the dominant input and its price is crude-linked, so the unit is really a spread business: buy yarn, convert, sell before the season turns. **When a proposal lands, check the yarn-to-blanket spread and the seasonality of receivables, not just turnover.**

## What has broken now
**Domestic demand is down nearly 50% this season and production is down 30-35% [3].** Yarn that cost Rs 100-105 per kg last year is now around Rs 155 per kg, and common mink blankets sell at Rs 210-240 per kg [3]. Peer Prakash Woollen shows the same squeeze: revenue up 45% but operating costs up 50%, leaving an operating loss of Rs 218.11 lakh, with profit only from a Rs 648.05 lakh NHAI land compensation [4][5]. **So when a proposal lands, strip out one-off income; if profit depends on an exceptional item, ask what the operating result was.** Fire risk is real and local — a blanket factory fire in Balana village with fire-safety equipment gaps [2].

## Where the growth is
**Haryana GST collections are running +10.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], and India-wide IIP for NIC 13 is +13.1% YoY [D].** That is a local tailwind, but the blanket segment is clearly the weak spot. Pursue integrated units with own dyeing/finishing, diversified into shawls and made-ups, and units selling to institutional or export buyers. Iris Clothings shows +40.3% YoY total income at a 15.2% EBITDA margin [6]; Arvind shows +23% revenue and +44% net profit [7] — both are larger, branded players, so read them as direction, not as Panipat comparables. **Avoid pure blanket converters with one stockist channel and no fire compliance.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash credit against stock and receivables with a drawing power recalculated monthly, plus a term loan only for fire-safety and finishing capex.** Rating methodology is explicit that weaving is fixed- and working-capital intensive and that low leverage protects through downturns [8][11]. Take monthly stock statements, quarterly GST returns, and yarn purchase invoices. **If the drawing power is being met only by revaluing old stock, ask for a physical inspection.**

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly stock statement (monthly):** stock ageing beyond one season -> cut drawing power and ask for stock liquidation plan.
- **GST returns (monthly):** turnover falling faster than the 50% industry dip [3] -> freeze fresh limits.
- **Yarn invoice prices (monthly):** purchase price moving above Rs 155 per kg [3] without matching sale price -> rework the spread.
- **Fire-safety certificate (annual):** no valid certificate -> no enhancement until compliance [2].
